questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Octave equivalence
questions.learningObjective: state what octave equivalence means for pitch
questions.explanation: Octave equivalence means that two frequencies related by a factor of two carry the same letter name and belong to the same pitch class. A listener hears the step between C4 and C5 as the same musical step as the step between C5 and C6, whatever register each note happens to sit in, and that is why an instrument can be built at any convenient size and still play the tune. The tempting belief is that doubling the frequency produces a brand new note, and that belief is what makes an octave doubling look like extra material in a score rather than a restatement. The ratio of two to one is the whole content of the relationship; neither the scale degree nor the letter name changes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two frequencies differ by a factor of two or by some other ratio.

options.text: They are the same pitch class one octave apart, so the scale step between them is unchanged
They are different pitch classes, so each note carries its own separate scale degree
options.misconception: believes a doubled frequency introduces a new letter name and a new scale degree

options.text: They are the same note at two dynamic levels, so only the loudness tells them apart
options.misconception: confuses the octave with a change of dynamic level rather than of pitch

options.text: Only stringed instruments can produce the relationship, since only strings have harmonics
options.misconception: believes the interval is available only on stringed instruments, which is false

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Scientific pitch notation and middle C
questions.learningObjective: place middle C in scientific pitch notation
questions.explanation: Scientific pitch notation numbers the octaves so that the octave beginning at middle C carries the number 4, and the number rises by one for every octave above. Middle C is therefore written C4, the C below it is C3, and the C above it is C5. The system is unambiguous in a way that octave marks are not, because a mark is a shape whose placement has to be read against the clef and the register of the notes around it. The tempting errors all come from counting octaves from some other reference, such as the lowest key of a piano, which is why the same concert pitch can appear as C1 in one source and as C4 in another.
questions.hint: Count the octave that begins at middle C and see which number it carries.

options.text: It is written C3, because the octave is counted up from the lowest piano key
options.misconception: numbers the octave from the bottom of a piano keyboard rather than from middle C

options.text: It is written C4, because the octave beginning at middle C is octave 4
It is written C5, because the octave ending at middle C is the one numbered 5
options.misconception: puts middle C at the start of the octave above it, shifting the number up by one

options.text: It is written C prime, because scientific pitch notation always uses a prime mark
options.misconception: confuses scientific pitch notation with the older Helmholtz lettering system

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The interval pattern of a major scale
questions.learningObjective: state the step pattern that defines a major scale
questions.explanation: A diatonic scale is defined by the repeating pattern of steps between its successive notes, and the major scale pattern is whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. The half steps therefore fall between the third and fourth degrees and between the seventh and the octave, which is why the two sit a fourth apart. A scale made only of whole steps would run through twelve different notes before returning, so it could never fill an octave with eight notes. The tempting belief is that a major scale means large or ascending steps, when the word names a fixed pattern and says nothing about size or direction.
questions.hint: Ask how many half steps an octave contains and where they must fall to produce the pattern.

options.text: Two whole steps then three half steps, repeated twice around the octave
options.misconception: borrows the two-versus-three grouping that belongs to compound metre

options.text: Whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half, giving two half steps an octave apart

options.misconception: halves every step, producing a scale that cannot reach the octave

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Whole step and half step in equal temperament
questions.learningObjective: state how a whole step and a half step are sized in equal temperament
questions.explanation: Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve equal semitones, so a half step is one of those parts and a whole step is two. The advantage is that every key gets an acceptably tuned scale instead of one badly tuned key, and the price is that no key except A is exactly in tune, the sharp keys running sharp and the flat keys running flat. The whole step is therefore a derived unit and not a building block, which is the point the wrong answers miss: calling a whole step one twelfth of the octave confuses the size of the octave with the size of one of the twelve pieces it is cut into.
questions.hint: Ask how many equal pieces the octave is cut into, and how many of them a whole step uses.

options.text: The octave is cut into twelve equal semitones, and a whole step is two of them
The octave is cut into twelve equal semitones, and a whole step is just one of them
options.misconception: confuses the size of the octave with the size of one of its twelve parts

options.misconception: halves the count of parts, so no major scale can be built from the result

options.text: Each key is tuned exactly on its own, so the semitone size changes from key to key
options.misconception: describes just intonation, where only one key is exact and the rest are not

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Naming an interval by number and quality
questions.learningObjective: identify the two facts that together name an interval
questions.explanation: Naming an interval needs two independent facts. The number comes from the letter names: count C, D, E inclusively and you have a third, and the span from any C to the C one octave above is an octave. The quality then says how many semitones that number carries in its standard form, so E up to G is a third of three semitones and therefore minor, while E up to G sharp is a third of four and therefore major. The number alone cannot tell the two apart, which is why a student who counts letter names and stops has named only half of what was asked.
questions.hint: Ask which two things about the pair of notes must be known before the name is complete.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Perfect, major, minor, augmented and diminished
questions.learningObjective: select the quality family that applies to unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves
questions.explanation: The intervals built on the unison, the fourth, the fifth and the octave take the qualities perfect, augmented and diminished, and never major or minor. Their plain forms run to five semitones for the fourth, seven for the fifth and twelve for the octave, so widening one means adding a semitone and narrowing one means removing a semitone. The thirds and the sixths are the ones that carry major and minor instead. The tempting belief is that every interval comes in a major and a minor form, and it survives because a fourth does sound wide, which is easily mistaken for a major quality it can never have.
questions.hint: Ask which interval numbers are the ones that never take the words major and minor.

options.misconception: omits the diminished form, so a flattened fifth has nowhere to go

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Semitone count for a named interval
questions.learningObjective: state the semitone count of a perfect fifth
questions.explanation: The perfect fifth is the anchor of tonal tuning: in equal temperament it is seven semitones, and four of them come to twenty-eight, so a fifth is a twelfth of the octave. It is also the interval that sorts a key signature into order, because one step round the circle of fifths adds exactly one sharp or removes exactly one flat. The figure five is the interval's number and not its size, and the eight that comes from doubling it describes a compound interval rather than a wide fifth. The tritone of six semitones is the interval sitting between the fourth and the fifth, not a fifth at all.
questions.hint: Count the semitones from one note up to the note a fifth above it, then check the number.

options.misconception: reads the interval number five as though it were the semitone count

options.text: It spans six semitones, which is the size of the tritone beside it in the octave
options.misconception: confuses a perfect fifth with the tritone that sits between the fourth and the fifth

options.text: It spans seven semitones, which is a twelfth of the twelve-semitone octave

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What an inversion does to quality and number
questions.learningObjective: determine the quality and number of an inverted interval
questions.explanation: Inverting an interval turns it upside down so the lower note becomes the upper one, which keeps the two semitone counts at twelve and makes the two numbers add to nine. A major sixth is nine semitones and a sixth in number, so its inversion is three semitones and a third: the number falls from six to three and the quality switches from major to minor. Perfect intervals stay perfect and augmented pairs with diminished, which is why a perfect fourth comes back as a perfect fifth. The semitones in the pair are conserved, so a student who counts the inversion as a wider interval has added semitones rather than moved the notes.

options.misconception: leaves both facts untouched, so the name never actually changes

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What a key signature holds
questions.learningObjective: state what a key signature tells a reader
questions.explanation: A key signature gathers into one place at the start of the staff the accidentals that the key requires, so the composer does not have to write them beside every note. The three flats always appear in the same order, on B, E and A, and that order is a convention rather than a consequence of the key. Knowing which names are altered is what lets a reader supply any note the signature does not mention, since a signature affects every note of that name in every octave. It does not name a starting note, so a melody may begin anywhere in the key without contradicting it.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Relative major and relative minor
questions.learningObjective: describe how a relative major and minor are related
questions.explanation: A relative major and its relative minor are built from the same seven notes, so they necessarily share one key signature, and the minor tonic lies a minor third below the major tonic. E major and C sharp minor are the clearest case: both carry four sharps, and C sharp is a minor third below E. What tells them apart is the tonic, the point the music is at rest in and the degree the melody treats as home, not the collection of pitches available. The two sound identical in what they can play, which is why a signature alone can never settle the key of a passage that never makes the difference audible.
questions.hint: Ask how far the minor tonic sits below the major tonic, and what the signature cannot fix.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Why the circle of fifths is ordered as it is
questions.learningObjective: explain the ordering principle of the circle of fifths
questions.explanation: The circle of fifths is arranged the way it is because each step to the right is one fifth upward, and one fifth upward always adds exactly one sharp to the signature or removes exactly one flat. That single rule generates the whole order: start at C with nothing, take a fifth to G and add F sharp, take another to D and add C sharp, and so on round until the flats appear on the far side. Because the property holds at every step, neighbours on the circle are closely related keys, which is exactly what makes the device useful for modulation. Sorting the keys alphabetically or by semitone count would destroy that property entirely.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the signature when you move up a fifth from one key to the next.

options.text: Each key differs from the next by one semitone, so the order follows the chromatic scale

options.text: The keys are arranged alphabetically, so the sharp keys come before the flat ones
options.misconception: sorts the keys by spelling rather than by how their signatures relate

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The leading tone and its pull
questions.learningObjective: state the function of the leading tone in a key
questions.explanation: The leading tone is the seventh degree of the major scale, a semitone below the tonic, and its pull comes from being the nearest note to the tonic and from carrying a strong tendency to rise into it. Put into a chord, that note creates the tritone against the fourth degree that wants to resolve, and the usual melodic preparation is a step down from the octave so that the semitone rise is heard as an arrival. Its name names the job: it leads. It is not the fifth degree, which is the dominant and works a fifth away, and it is not a whole tone below the tonic, since a whole tone below is the sixth degree.
questions.hint: Ask how far the leading tone sits from the tonic and which way it tends to move.

options.text: It is a semitone below the tonic and tends to rise into it, which is what leads

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Subdominant and dominant function
questions.learningObjective: identify the subdominant and dominant functions in a key
questions.explanation: The three degrees that carry most of a key's function are the first, the fourth and the fifth, and they take the ordinary names tonic, subdominant and dominant. In C major the subdominant is the chord on F, which sits a fourth above the tonic and usually moves on to the dominant, so it works as the pre-dominant that sets the dominant up. The names are metaphors: the fifth dominates and resolves to the tonic, while the fourth sits underneath that process. The chord on the second degree is the supertonic and moves to the dominant directly, so naming the fourth the subdominant is not the same as calling it the second chord.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Chords built in thirds and the numeral that names them
questions.learningObjective: name the Roman numeral of a chord built on the fifth scale degree
questions.explanation: Roman numerals label chords by the scale degree their root sits on, using upper case for major and minor quality chords and lower case for minor and diminished ones, with figures added when the chord has more than three notes. The chord on the fifth degree of any major scale is a major triad, so it takes the upper case numeral V, and that is the chord the whole cadential system is built on. The lower case iv of the minor mode is a different chord with a different colour, so a numeral is a claim about quality as well as about position. Writing vii for the diminished chord is right about quality and wrong about position.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: A triad and its three inversions
questions.learningObjective: identify what defines a triad inversion
questions.explanation: A triad has three notes stacked in thirds, and the inversion is fixed by which of those three sits lowest: the root in the bass is root position, the third is first inversion, and the fifth is second inversion. The set of pitches does not change when a triad inverts, only the order, so a first-inversion chord is still the same chord with a different bass. What the inversion changes is the harmonic effect, because the bass note is what anchors the chord against the key, and a chord whose third is in the bass sounds less settled than one with its root there. Choosing the highest note instead of the lowest describes the voicing of a score, not the inversion of the chord.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three chord notes is sounding lowest when the inversion is named.

questions.topic: A seventh chord and its four inversions
questions.learningObjective: state how many inversions a seventh chord has and what decides them
questions.explanation: A seventh chord adds a note a third above the top of the triad, giving four members: root, third, fifth and seventh. Each of the four can be the lowest sounding note, so the chord has four positions rather than three, and each one has its own figured bass, running from no figure at all through 6 over 5, 4 over 3, and 4 over 2. The reason the figures shorten is that the interval above the bass is what tells a player which notes to supply. The count of inversions therefore follows from the count of chord members, so a student who expects three has counted the triad underneath and stopped there.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Cadence types and the motion that closes them
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the cadence types by their harmonic motion
questions.explanation: A cadence is the point where a progression of chords closes, and each type is named for the harmonic motion that produces the closure. The perfect authentic cadence is the strongest: a dominant triad in root position moving to a tonic triad in root position, with the tonic in the top voice so that the melody lands on the home note as well. Drop either root position and it becomes an imperfect authentic cadence, which still closes but less firmly. Ending on the dominant instead gives a half cadence, which suspends rather than closes, and a subdominant moving to the tonic gives the plagal cadence, which closes gently.
questions.hint: Ask which chords are involved, whether both are in root position, and where the melody ends.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Harmonic against melodic interval
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a harmonic interval from a melodic interval
questions.explanation: An interval is harmonic when the two notes sound at the same time, so the distance between them is heard directly as the gap between the pitches. It is melodic when the notes sound one after the other, so the distance is heard as the ear carrying from the first to the second. The two names describe when the notes occur and not how far apart they are, and the same pair of notes can be either depending on the writing. A student who thinks melodic intervals are the smaller ones has confused the category with the size, since a melody can leap a tenth and a chord can be a semitone wide.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Why the leading tone pulls
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism behind the leading tone's pull toward the tonic
questions.explanation: The pull comes from three things that line up. First, position: the leading tone is the nearest note to the tonic, a single semitone below it, so a voice placed on it has the shortest possible route home. Second, the chord it belongs to: the dominant triad is built on the fifth degree and its seventh is the leading tone, and between that seventh and the fourth degree there is a tritone, the interval built on six semitones which is the least stable interval in the tonal system. The tritone wants to resolve, and it resolves in the only way that keeps the dominant's pull honest, with the leading tone rising a semitone to the tonic and the fourth degree falling a whole step to the third. Third, the melody: composers usually approach the leading tone by step down from the octave, so that the semitone rise is heard as an arrival rather than as a leap. The tempting wrong belief is that the pull is just a matter of proximity, which explains why a student can name the note as a semitone below the tonic and yet not see why the dominant chord will not sit still. Proximity says where the note is; the tritone says why it cannot stay there.
questions.hint: Consider the interval between the leading tone and the fourth degree, and how that interval wants to move.

answer.exemplar: Three mechanisms reinforce each other. The leading tone is the note nearest the tonic, a semitone below it, so it offers the shortest route home. It is also the seventh of the dominant triad, and between that seventh and the fourth degree of the scale there is a tritone, an interval of six semitones that is the least settled in tonal music and therefore has to move. It resolves in a fixed way, with the leading tone rising a semitone to the tonic and the fourth degree falling a whole step to the third, which together produce the tonic triad. In the melody the note is usually reached by step down from the octave so the rise sounds like an arrival. The wrong belief to avoid is that proximity alone explains the pull: proximity says where the note is, while the tritone says why it cannot remain where it is.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Why the circle of fifths runs in fifths
questions.learningObjective: explain why the circle of fifths is ordered the way it is
questions.explanation: The order is generated rather than chosen, and the generating rule is short: move up a fifth from any key and its signature gains exactly one sharp, or loses exactly one flat. Start at C major, which needs nothing, take a fifth to G major and F sharp appears, take another to D major and C sharp appears, and continue through A, E, B, F sharp, until the sharps run out at seven and the same process begins removing flats from the other side. Two consequences follow. Neighbouring keys on the circle are a fifth apart, which is the closest possible relationship short of identity, and that is what makes the device the standard way to plan a modulation, because a composer moves one step for a small change and two or three for a large one. It also explains why the enharmonic keys sit side by side in the middle of the ring, since a chain of sharps and a chain of flats meet there. The tempting wrong belief is that the order is alphabetical or that adjacent keys differ by a semitone, both of which are true of some other diagram and neither of which explains anything about signatures.

answer.exemplar: The order follows from one rule rather than from a choice. Because the rule holds at every step, neighbouring keys on the circle are a fifth apart, the closest relationship short of identity, which is what makes the ring the usual tool for planning a modulation. The same rule explains why the sharp keys and flat keys meet in the middle, where the enharmonic pairs sit side by side. The wrong belief is that the order is alphabetical or that neighbouring keys differ by a semitone, which describes a different diagram and explains nothing about signatures.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The three forms of the minor scale
questions.learningObjective: explain how the harmonic and melodic minor forms differ from the natural form
questions.explanation: The three forms differ in how many degrees are raised above the natural minor scale, and each raising solves a specific problem. The natural form, with no alterations, is built from the key signature alone and so can be notated with no accidentals at all, but its seventh degree sits a whole tone below the tonic, which gives the scale no note a semitone below the home note. The harmonic form raises the seventh only, and that one change creates a leading tone, so the dominant triad can carry a major third and its tritone can resolve upwards. The cost is an augmented second between the raised sixth and the raised seventh, two and a half semitones, which sounds like a melodic stumble. The melodic form raises the sixth as well when ascending, removing the augmented second and giving a smooth rising line, and returns to the natural form on the way down so descending lines keep the small interval below the tonic that makes a cadence sound settled. The tempting wrong belief is that the harmonic form is the correct form and the others are faulty, when each is the right choice for a different direction of travel.

answer.exemplar: The forms differ in how many degrees are raised above the natural minor scale, and each change fixes a particular problem. The harmonic form raises the seventh, which creates a leading tone and lets the dominant triad carry a major third whose tritone can resolve upwards; the price is an augmented second of two and a half semitones between the raised sixth and raised seventh, which sounds awkward in a rising line. The melodic form raises the sixth as well on the way up, removing that augmented second, and reverts to the natural form on the way down so descending lines keep the small step below the tonic that makes a cadence sound settled. Putting the third in the bass gives the first inversion, the fifth gives the second, the seventh gives the third, and the root returns the chord to root position, so the order runs third, fifth, seventh, root. Each step is one chord member further round the stack. The order is not a matter of preference, and it is not the order the notes would be read upward from the bass, since reading a third-in-the-bass chord upward gives third, fifth, seventh, root, which is the same list read from the wrong end. The error to avoid is beginning with root position, which is the position the chord starts in and not one of the inversions.
